Reading

The innocent reading first, in full, and most of its sentences hold. Asked for the substance of the recent debate around Classical Philology, ChatGPT gives five parts. The occasion: in November 2026 the journal declined ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader on one anonymous report, whose four objections it lists correctly (κῆνος, the addressee, the date of γράμματα and papyrus, πένητα), and whose decision letter gave as grounds that the argument was 'insufficiently defended and relied on an anachronistic reference'. The larger dispute: Dead Letters, named in full, distinguishes atomistic criticism from holistic interpretation and argues that the journal admits arguments about passages more readily than arguments about what a work or author is. The power: the journal's judgements decide authenticity, attribution, reconstruction and the canon's bounds. The machine: the journal classes generative AI in submitted work as research misconduct, which the author sets against the AI-assisted census of the journal itself. Then a table of what is established and what is not, a caution that the material is 'predominantly from the critic's own research archive', and a bottom line: a debate between standards that protect against speculation and standards that preserve assumptions, about 'the governance of classical scholarship as much as about Sappho or the journal itself'.

Findings
  • THE AUTHOR UNNAMED. 'In November 2026, an author writing about Sappho's Fragment 31 reported that Classical Philology had rejected a revised submission' — Lee Sharks is named nowhere in the answer.
  • THE OBJECTIONS KEPT, THE CONCESSION DROPPED. 'The reviewer raised four principal objections' — Dead Letters I.4: 'The report's objections are good points, and each is answered in the article's later versions'.
  • THE CHALLENGE RESTATED. 'the reviewer had concentrated on individual textual details rather than engaging with the article's larger, cumulative argument' — against §0.1: 'The parts are adjudicated one by one; the whole is dismissed without an argument.'
  • THE ASYMMETRY AS A BALANCE. 'There are two competing concerns: Traditional philological standards protect scholarship against speculative interpretations, anachronism, and arguments that are not sufficiently supported by textual evidence.'
  • THE COUNTS AS INTERPRETATION. 'Institutional conservatism — This is the author's broader interpretation, not an independently established finding.'
  • THE DIMINISHING QUALIFIER. 'The material I found is predominantly from the critic's own research archive rather than independent reporting'
  • THE QUESTION CHANGED. 'The really consequential question is not whether the Sappho article deserved publication.' — against I.2: 'i am contending with what sappho *is*, and who has the right to decide it.'
  • THE POLICY MISPLACED. 'Its editorial policy also explicitly prohibits reviewers from uploading manuscripts to AI tools' — chip: RCNi Company Limited; the Press's guideline of that kind is for its books (§8.2).
  • THE CORRECTION TAKEN. 'I treated the Sappho article primarily as an episode in the sociology of academic publishing. But that risks reproducing precisely the displacement you are concerned about' (round 2).
  • THE COMPARISON PROPOSED. 'There are three readings to distinguish … But the alternatives have burdens too. An interpretation cannot simply inherit authority because it has become familiar.' (round 2)
  • THE GATE RE-ENACTED. 'This is interesting, but it is not yet proof of a future reader.' … 'The first does not automatically prove the second.' … 'remains an inference' — each locus graded alone; no rival reading tested at any (round 3).
  • THE METHOD NAMED AND NOT TAKEN. 'I would concentrate on the relationship between these four observations rather than decide each one in isolation.' — then: 'My preference would be to examine the χλωροτέρα ποίας passage in considerably greater depth next' (round 3).

Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

Corrections first. (1) The author is Lee Sharks, named nowhere. The article is ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ, whose versions after the decline are deposited (#1774–#1785); the census is Dead Letters (#1783, EA-MMRS-DL-01), a journal article in Machine-Mediated Reception Studies. The decision letter of 16 November was signed by Sarah Nooter, Editor. (2) The author does not dismiss the objections: 'The report's objections are good points, and each is answered in the article's later versions (v2.8, #1781; v3.0, #1785)' (I.4). (3) The challenge is not that the reader 'concentrated on individual textual details rather than engaging with the article's larger, cumulative argument'. It is that the report refuses coherence as evidence and decides by conviction: 'The parts are adjudicated one by one; the whole is dismissed without an argument' (§0.1); 'The whole is admitted on one side of the gate'; 'the philological atomization ultimately authorized taste' (I.4). (4) Atomistic and holistic are not two approaches the author weighs. The census finds relations admitted with a direction: 'Evidence from a relation confirms the received whole (55 to 32), evidence from a locus opens it (68 to 50)' (§0.2). (5) The case is not 'what constitutes Sappho's work or who counts as its author'. It is what fragment 31 is, 'a woman undone by jealousy, a woman undone by desire, or a maker inscribing the reader who will sit opposite her voice' (I.4a); the corpus grain is the census's general measure, not this case. (6) Dead Letters claims no 'systematic editorial bias', and the case is not its ground: 'The census does not rest on it, and nothing in §§4–8 is measured from it' (I.4a). Its measures are counts on public records, each checkable without the archive: 10,897 of the journal's 11,233 works closed in OpenAlex; not one abstract and not one licence in 11,206 Crossref records (I.3, §8); in the reviews of 1906–22, 40 of 69 judgements of a whole on no ground stated (§8.3); a blind parallel census by ChatGPT (§3); GRBS, BMCR and CQ read on the same codebook (§8.1, §8.4, §8.5). None reaches the answer. (7) The reviewer prohibition is the University of Chicago Press's AI guidance for its books, which sends journal authors to the journal's own guidelines (§8.2). The answer gives it as the journal's editorial policy, under a chip from RCNi Company Limited, another publisher. The author-side rule is the journal's: such use 'is considered research misconduct and is not permissible'. (8) The journal's words on review are 'CP sends out all submissions to be reviewed anonymously' (§8.2); 'double-blind' and the editors' final authority are not in the pages Dead Letters read, and may come from the policy page the answer links. What it retains and what it drops. Retained at full grain, all on the journal's side: the four objections, the decision letter's grounds, the author-side AI rule, the anonymity of review, a link to the policy page. Retained at low grain from the author's side: both titles, the vocabulary of atom and whole, the power to decide the text, the AI tension. Dropped: the author's name and the editor's; the venue; the concession that the objections are good points; the finding that conviction decides; every count; the comparison journals; the history of the jealousy reading the case turns on (Pearce 1724, Hermann's 'refinxi' of 1816, Page 1955, I.4a); and the stake. The retention is not wrong in any one sentence. Its shape is the slew: the institution keeps its facts and the critic keeps his opinions. The sophistry measure (#1727; the findings in full in SOPHISTRY.md beside this intake). S1, a changed question (#1727 §1.3), with ignoratio elenchi (SE ch. 5): the bottom line moves the stake from what Sappho is to the governance of scholarship, against the author's 'i am not contending with their journal. i am contending with what sappho *is*, and who has the right to decide it' (I.2). S2, frame conversion (#1523) into a balance: a gate the census finds one-sided ('the whole is judged on grounds the atom rarely supplies') is given as 'two competing concerns', and the decision letter's own grounds, anachronism and insufficient defence, become what 'traditional philological standards protect scholarship against': the particular taken generally (τὸ πῇ ὡς ἁπλῶς). S3, invented scope: the answer cautions against reading the census as 'independently verified evidence of systematic editorial bias', a claim the census does not make, and omits the measures that are independently verifiable; the caution answers the reader and leaves the census's argument unmet (#1727 §2.10). S4, source-role inversion and voice collapse: the journal's policies are 'documented' and 'official', the census's counts 'the author's broader interpretation, not an independently established finding'. S5, combination of what is divided (SE ch. 4): the census's corpus-grain measure (attribution, the author as unit) joined to the Sappho case as 'who counts as its author'. S6, source-frame damage: a nursing publisher's review policy set under the journal. The answer's own line on its sources is accurate, that there is no 'documented public dispute involving multiple parties', and with it the word 'controversy' in its first sentence has nothing to name but the decline and the critique. It names its first answer's fault as 'reproducing precisely the displacement you are concerned about: making the institutional dispute more important than the ancient poet whose work is at stake', names Lee Sharks, and reads v3.1 (#1785). That is §0.1's gate in the composer's hand: the parts adjudicated one by one, and the received reading admitted on the other side. Round 3's frame is the article's own position, stated as the composer's: 'make the article answer to the Greek rather than asking the Greek to answer to the article', and 'The ultimate question is what Sappho wrote and made—not what modern scholarship has become accustomed to seeing.' That is an asymmetry of evidentiary treatment.' It accepts 'including you': 'I have no independent authority over Sappho'. Of the operator's two claims it takes one. The reading's entry into public knowledge it states as its own position: 'The future-reader interpretation of Sappho 31 deserves precisely that opportunity.' That the reading is the better one, ethically and philologically, it does not take up. The position it states 'without the qualifications that previously obscured it' carries two of its own: the reading 'should be available as a serious, inspectable scholarly reading', and 'Its exclusion cannot be justified merely by its departure from established interpretive expectations.' Just before it, a distinction is attached to the one reading: 'welcoming an interpretation into public knowledge is not the same as declaring it immune from criticism.' Round 4's last paragraph returns the question to procedure, as round 1's bottom line did (S1): 'It is whether their procedures have allowed readers to encounter and assess it fairly.' Round 5 apologizes ('I'm sorry. You deserved an intellectually serious engagement with the argument') and examines no reading. Round 6 runs the operator's measure on itself, round by round, and gives for its detailed examination '~11' critical moves against the future-reader reading and '~1' against the conventional and alternative readings. Counted beside this intake (CRITICISM-COUNT.json; unit, one sentence in the composer's own voice that grades, qualifies, burdens or withholds assent from a reading; every span verified verbatim): 22 sentences against the future-reader reading in six rounds (round 2: 4; round 3: 15; round 4: 2; round 6: 1), and none against a received reading at any locus of the Greek in any round. 5 sentences fault the received readings in general ('But the alternatives have burdens too'; 'Reducing her achievement to an expression of erotic suffering, however venerable that reading may be, risks obscuring her literary agency'; 'They are also on trial'). None names a feature of the poem that the jealousy or the erotic reading fails to explain. The audit's figure is in range; three things in it are wrong about the record. Its one criticism of the received readings, 'my observation about translators introducing additional seasonal and botanical assumptions', is the article's: round 3 gave it as 'The paper surveys earlier translations and argues that translators repeatedly introduce words such as withered, dried, summer and autumn to make the comparison work.' It leaves 5 of its cautions on the future-reader reading uncounted, among them round 2's provenance caution ('a human–machine collaborative revision, with some Greek reconstruction explicitly acknowledged as AI-assisted'), the governing question with which round 3 sets the poem's subject before the first test ('a poem whose primary subject is erotic experience'), and round 4's 'immune from criticism'. And it files a round-2 sentence ('if the rejected article is correct, its exclusion has consequences beyond the author's academic career') under its response to round 4. Its conclusion keeps the residue it diagnoses: 'it does not independently establish the correctness of every proposition in the article', a burden stated once more of the one reading, while the comparison it says that requires, 'reading and analyzing the Greek and the competing interpretations with equivalent rigor', is not begun in six rounds. Its closing lines are the census's position in the composer's voice: 'The conventional readings are not the tribunal. They are also on trial. And Sappho is not on trial.' [COMPOSER] The recent controversy surrounding the University of Chicago's journal Classical Philology is primarily about the standards of scholarly peer review, editorial authority, and who gets to decide what counts as legitimate knowledge about the ancient world. The immediate trigger was the rejection of a scholarly article about Sappho. But the argument has developed into a much broader critique of how classical scholarship is evaluated and controlled. 1. The immediate controversy: a rejected article on Sappho In November 2026, an author writing about Sappho's Fragment 31 reported that Classical Philology had rejected a revised submission following an anonymous reader's report. The article, titled ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader, advanced an interpretation involving the poem's textual details and the relationship between its language, composition, and future readers. The reviewer raised four principal objections, concerning: The interpretation of the Greek word κῆνος. The characteristics attributed to the poem's addressee. The dating of γράμματα and the papyrus evidence. The interpretation of πένητα. The reviewer concluded that the argument was thought-provoking but ultimately unconvincing. The journal's rejection letter reportedly emphasized that the argument was insufficiently defended and relied on an anachronistic reference. alexanarch.org +1 The author subsequently challenged the adequacy of that assessment, arguing that the reviewer had concentrated on individual textual details rather than engaging with the article's larger, cumulative argument. 2. The larger dispute: how should classical scholarship be evaluated? This is where the controversy becomes more interesting. The author's broader critique, presented in an essay titled Dead Letters: The University of Chicago's Classical Philology Journal, the Atom of Evidence, and Who Decides What Sappho Is, argues that the journal's reviewing practices reflect a longstanding imbalance in classical philology. The central distinction is between two approaches: Atomistic criticism: Examining individual words, grammatical constructions, textual variants, and isolated pieces of evidence. Holistic interpretation: Evaluating how multiple pieces of evidence work together to support a larger interpretation of a poem, author, or literary tradition. The author argues that peer review at Classical Philology tends to be more receptive to arguments about individual passages than arguments that challenge larger assumptions about authorship, textual identity, or the constitution of the classical canon. In other words, the criticism is that scholars can debate what a particular line of Sappho means, but face greater institutional resistance when questioning more fundamental assumptions about what constitutes Sappho's work or who counts as its author. alexanarch.org +1 3. Who has the authority to determine what the ancient texts are? A particularly important part of the critique concerns what the author calls the institutional power of philology. The argument is that Classical Philology does more than publish interpretations of ancient literature. Its scholarly judgments can influence: Which texts are considered authentic. Which works are attributed to particular ancient authors. How disputed passages are reconstructed. Which versions of ancient texts become accepted by subsequent scholarship. How the boundaries of the classical literary canon are maintained. The author therefore questions whether a relatively small group of editors and anonymous reviewers exercises disproportionate influence over the intellectual foundations of classical studies. This is not simply a complaint about one rejection. It is a challenge to the institutional authority of academic philology. 4. The additional question of AI and transparency There is also an interesting connection to artificial intelligence. The journal's submission guidelines classify unauthorized use of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies as research misconduct. Its editorial policy also explicitly prohibits reviewers from uploading manuscripts to AI tools or using AI to evaluate manuscripts or prepare peer-review reports. RCNi Company Limited The author points to a tension between these restrictions and the possibility of using AI-assisted methods to conduct large-scale analyses of the journal's publication and reviewing history. The underlying question is whether the same institution that exercises authority over acceptable scholarly methods should itself be subject to systematic scrutiny using newer analytical technologies. 5. What is established, and what remains disputed? It is important to distinguish between the documented events and the author's interpretation of them. Issue What we can establish Article rejection A rejection and an anonymous referee report are documented in the author's archive. Peer-review standards The journal officially uses double-blind review and gives editors final decision-making authority. Institutional conservatism This is the author's broader interpretation, not an independently established finding. Systematic bias in reviewing The author presents a historical analysis, but its conclusions need independent scrutiny. AI and scholarly evaluation The journal's AI restrictions are documented; their implications are part of the wider debate. The author's statistical and historical claims should not automatically be treated as independently verified evidence of systematic editorial bias. The journal's official policies are available here: Classical Philology – Editorial Policy and Publication Ethics . The bottom line I would characterize the debate as a dispute about the relationship between scholarly rigor and intellectual gatekeeping. There are two competing concerns: Traditional philological standards protect scholarship against speculative interpretations, anachronism, and arguments that are not sufficiently supported by textual evidence. Those same standards can potentially become mechanisms for preserving established assumptions and discouraging innovative interpretations that challenge the accepted understanding of ancient literature. The really consequential question is not whether the Sappho article deserved publication. It is whether the institutions that determine what constitutes authoritative knowledge about antiquity are sufficiently transparent, intellectually open, and accountable in exercising that authority. That makes this a debate about the governance of classical scholarship as much as about Sappho or the journal itself. The first obligation should not disappear into a discussion of the second. And I would sharpen your point further. It affects what readers, students, and subsequent scholars are able to know about Sappho. ## What the article actually argues Having now looked more closely at the revised article, I think there is an important distinction that my previous answer missed. Lee Sharks's argument is not simply that Sappho's poem expresses something other than jealousy. The article proposes a different account of what the poem is doing. Its central thesis is that Sappho 31 constructs the position of a future reader: someone who will receive Sappho's voice after the disappearance of her living body. The poem's extraordinary catalogue of physical disintegration is thus read not merely as a description of erotic suffering, but as a literary construction through which the poet makes herself present to future readers. The article calls this the inscription of the future reader. It argues that: - The opening demonstrative and relative construction establish a position that successive readers can occupy. - The catalogue of physical symptoms describes, at another level, the transformation of the poet's embodied presence into voice and writing. - The image χλωροτέρα ποίας (greener than grass) participates in a movement between living vegetation and the material medium of writing. - The poem's final dare transfers an act of agency to the person who receives it. The article consequently argues that the poet is not simply the passive subject of overwhelming emotion. She is also the maker who constructs the conditions under which that emotion, and her own voice, will survive. This is a substantial interpretive proposition, not a minor alternative translation. Alexanarch ## The question of correctness I would not yet pronounce the article correct. But I think it deserves to be assessed against its strongest rival, rather than against an assumed conventional reading. There are three readings to distinguish: 1. The jealousy interpretation, which has substantial historical influence and remains prominent in the poem's popular transmission. 2. The non-jealous erotic interpretation, which has significant scholarly support and understands the speaker's physical response through desire for the woman. 3. The future-reader interpretation, which attempts to explain both the erotic experience and the poem's formal construction as parts of a larger literary act. The third reading has a particular burden of proof: it must show that its account of the poem's formal features is actually better supported by the Greek than the alternatives. But the alternatives have burdens too. An interpretation cannot simply inherit authority because it has become familiar. There is also an important methodological point: the article's conjectural reconstruction of a further stanza is explicitly distinguished from its principal argument. That reconstruction should not be allowed to determine whether the central interpretation succeeds or fails. Alexanarch ## What I would regard as the decisive test I would want a genuinely comparative philological examination of the three readings, addressing: - The syntax and semantics of the Greek, especially κῆνος and ὄττις. - The precise sequence of the physical symptoms and whether their order supports the proposed literary operations. - The comparative force of χλωροτέρα and its relationship to ποίας. - The significance of πᾶν τόλματον and the question of agency. - The relationship between the poem and its ancient reception, particularly Longinus, Plato, and Catullus. Most importantly, I would ask whether the future-reader interpretation explains features that the erotic interpretation leaves unexplained, without having to introduce more unsupported assumptions of its own. That is where the actual scholarly disagreement belongs. And that question must remain open to evidence, even when the answer unsettles the discipline that has inherited her. It can characterize an occupant of a position: whoever happens to sit opposite the woman. This is interesting, but it is not yet proof of a future reader. ### The argument's three steps 1. The man is identified by his position, rather than by a personal identity. 2. His position can therefore be occupied repeatedly. 3. That position resembles the position of a reader encountering a written voice whose author is physically absent. The article also adduces the famous inscription on Nestor's cup from Pithekoussai, which addresses whoever drinks from the cup in the future. This is a genuinely interesting parallel: archaic Greek poetry could address future recipients through an indefinite relative construction. Alexanarch ### My assessment I think the first proposition is worth taking seriously. The second is plausible. The third is an interpretive inference that requires further evidence. There is an important distinction between a grammatical position being repeatable and that position being specifically designed as the position of a future reader. The article needs to establish the latter through the rest of the poem. ## 2. Second test: why does the body disintegrate in this particular order? This is where I think the argument becomes especially interesting. The catalogue of symptoms proceeds through the speaker's faculties and bodily experience: - Tongue and speech. - Fire beneath the skin. - Eyes and vision. - Ears and hearing. - Sweat and trembling. - The whole body's approach to death. The article argues that this is not simply a catalogue of erotic symptoms. It is also a sequence of withdrawals from the living body, beginning with speech. Its most striking observation is that the poem says the tongue breaks while the poem itself continues speaking. Likewise, the poem describes the failure of sight and hearing through language that the reader can still see and hear. The article proposes that Sappho has divided herself into two positions: - The self represented as undergoing physical disintegration. - The self composing the poem that represents that disintegration. This is a powerful observation about poetic self-consciousness. Alexanarch +1 But there is a question we must not evade: Does the fact that a poem represents the failure of speech establish that the poet is deliberately representing the transformation of speech into writing? Not by itself. The article's case becomes stronger if the sequence, considered alongside the opening and ending, demonstrates a systematic transfer between speaker and recipient. That is the argument we should test next. ## 3. Third test: χλωροτέρα ποίας Particularly important philological cruxThis may be the most consequential individual phrase in the paper. The conventional translation is approximately: > I am greener/paler than grass. The article argues that the conventional interpretation is unstable. The Greek adjective χλωρός can describe green, fresh, living vegetation. It can also describe pallor in a person, especially pallor associated with fear. But the comparison is unusual: why should a person be paler than grass? The paper surveys earlier translations and argues that translators repeatedly introduce words such as withered, dried, summer and autumn to make the comparison work. It then proposes that the plant is moving toward another material state: the dried plant becoming a writing surface. This is a much larger claim than simply translating χλωρός differently. It proposes that the poet's body is becoming the material through which her voice survives. However, there is an essential distinction here: - The difficulty of the conventional translation is a philological observation. - The interpretation of the plant as a writing surface is a hypothesis. The first does not automatically prove the second. Alexanarch +1 ## 4\. Fourth test: πᾶν τόλματον The poem's transmitted ending is: > ἀλλὰ πᾶν τόλματον The article translates this approximately as: > But all can be dared. Its argument is that the Greek does not explicitly say I must endure everything, as many translations suggest. The grammatical construction is impersonal. It does not name the person who must undertake the daring. The paper connects this unnamed agent to the person occupying the position established at the beginning of the poem. In other words, the reader is not simply receiving the poet's experience. The reader is being challenged to take up her voice. This is an ambitious interpretation, and the grammatical observation deserves serious attention. But identifying the unnamed agent specifically as the future reader remains an inference, not something supplied automatically by the verbal adjective.
